prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "VALERO ENERGY CORP/TX" (ticker VLO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "VLO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Valero Energy Corporation
markets: Diesel, jet fuel and other distillates
Renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (Diamond Green Diesel JV)
Wholesale fuel supply to about 7,000 Valero-, Diamond Shamrock-, Shamrock-, Ultramar- and Beacon-branded outlets
Refined product exports to Latin America and Europe

mission.plain: Valero says the world needs reliable, affordable energy and it wants to supply it safely and efficiently while moving into low-carbon fuels.

about.plain: Valero buys crude oil and cooks it in giant factories called refineries to make gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. It runs 14 refineries in the US, Canada and the UK that can handle about 3 million barrels a day. It also makes ethanol from corn at 12 plants and, with a partner, turns used cooking oil and animal fat into diesel and airplane fuel that cause less pollution. It sells these fuels to gas stations, airlines, trucking firms and other companies.
about.customers: Fuel wholesalers, branded gas-station owners, airlines, railroads, trucking firms, other oil companies and buyers in other countries purchase its fuels.
about.everyday: If you fill up at a Valero gas station, or fly on a plane or ride in a truck using diesel or jet fuel, there is a good chance the fuel came from a Valero refinery.

money.plain: gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other oil products
corn ethanol for gasoline and animal-feed grains
diesel and naphtha made from waste fats and oils
cleaner jet fuel from the Port Arthur plant

result.summary: Valero has a real but narrow advantage: it is one of the largest and lowest-cost independent refiners, with complex Gulf Coast plants that can run cheap heavy and sour crudes and export to Latin America and Europe, and no new US refinery has been built in decades. But it sells commodity fuels at prices set by global markets, so its profits swing hugely with crack spreads (from a $1.4 billion loss in 2020 to $11.5 billion profit in 2022 and back to $2.3 billion in 2025).

pricingPower.evidence: Valero is a price taker: its refining margin jumped to $23.62 per barrel in Q2 2026 (H1 2026: $19.31) because of global supply shocks such as the 2026 Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption, not its own pricing decisions, while weak cracks cut FY2025 operating income to $3,181M from $15,690M in 2022 and revenue to $122,687M from $176,383M.

moats.evidence: About 7,000 outlets carry the Valero, Diamond Shamrock, Shamrock, Ultramar and Beacon brands, but gasoline is a commodity and Valero owns very few stations itself after spinning off CST Brands in 2013.
Wholesale and spot fuel buyers can switch suppliers easily; branded dealer contracts give some stickiness but no lasting lock-in.
More customers do not make Valero's fuels more valuable to other customers.

Its 14 high-complexity refineries with about 3 million barrels/day of throughput capacity, heavily on the US Gulf Coast, can process discounted heavy sour crude and benefit from cheap US natural gas; record 2025 mechanical availability of 97.5% and refining throughput of 2,950 thousand barrels/day in Q2 2026 support low unit costs.

Building a new US refinery is practically impossible (none of significant size since the 1970s) and closures such as Valero's own Benicia idling in April 2026 tighten supply, which protects existing well-placed plants.

Valero kept investing in refining while some integrated majors and European refiners shrank capacity, and added low-carbon fuels (renewable diesel, SAF) that it can produce with existing refinery know-how.

Industry-leading operations (employee TRIR 0.13 and refinery mechanical availability 97.5% in 2025, both company records) and a strong crude-sourcing and export optimisation team are difficult to copy quickly.
Its 50% stake in Diamond Green Diesel (with Darling Ingredients, which supplies waste-fat feedstock) and its Gulf Coast refinery sites with deep-water docks are valuable but not exclusive.

customers.evidence: Valero sells mostly through wholesale, rack and branded channels; around 7,000 branded outlets and long-standing export customers in Latin America show repeat business, but buyers choose largely on price and location and no NPS or retention data is published.

talent.evidence: Valero has about 9,900 employees, strong safety culture (nine OSHA VPP Star refineries) and has been named an Extel (formerly Institutional Investor) Most Honored Company nine years running, but it does not feature on major recent best-employer rankings and refining is not a magnet for top young talent.

product.evidence: Its fuels meet the same specifications as rivals' fuels, so the product is undifferentiated; Valero's edge is reliability and cost, and its Port Arthur DGD plant can upgrade about half of its 470 million gallons/year renewable diesel capacity to neat SAF.

competitors.name: Marathon Petroleum Corporation
competitors.note: Largest US refiner by capacity; competes in Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent and West Coast fuels and exports, also renewable diesel (Martinez).

competitors.name: Phillips 66
competitors.note: Large US refiner and fuels marketer (Phillips 66, Conoco, 76 brands) with Gulf Coast and Mid-Continent refineries and Rodeo renewable fuels.

competitors.name: Exxon Mobil Corporation
competitors.note: Integrated major with large Gulf Coast refineries (Baytown, Beaumont, Baton Rouge) and branded fuels.

competitors.name: Chevron Corporation
competitors.note: Integrated major with US Gulf Coast (Pasadena, Pascagoula) and West Coast refining and branded retail fuels.

competitors.name: HF Sinclair Corporation
competitors.note: Independent refiner in the Mid-Continent, Rockies and Southwest, also renewable diesel and Sinclair-branded fuels.

competitors.name: PBF Energy Inc.
competitors.note: Independent refiner on the East, Gulf and West Coasts; renewable diesel JV (St. Bernard Renewables).

competitors.name: Motiva Enterprises (Saudi Aramco)
competitors.note: Owns Port Arthur, the largest US refinery, competing directly with Valero's Gulf Coast plants and exports.

competitors.name: CITGO Petroleum Corporation
competitors.note: Gulf Coast (Lake Charles, Corpus Christi) and Midwest (Lemont) refiner with CITGO-branded stations.

competitors.name: Shell plc
competitors.note: Global refining, fuels trading and Shell-branded retail; competes in fuel supply and low-carbon fuels.

competitors.name: BP p.l.c.
competitors.note: US refineries (Whiting, Cherry Point) and BP/Amoco/ARCO branded fuels.

competitors.name: Delek US Holdings, Inc.
competitors.note: Smaller independent refiner in Texas, Arkansas and the Permian region.

competitors.name: CVR Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Mid-Continent refiner (Coffeyville, Wynnewood) competing with Valero's Ardmore and McKee plants.

competitors.name: Reliance Industries Limited
competitors.note: Operates the world's largest refining complex at Jamnagar, competing for diesel and gasoline exports to Europe and Latin America.

competitors.name: Neste Oyj
competitors.note: World's largest renewable diesel and SAF producer, competing with Diamond Green Diesel for feedstocks and customers.

competitors.name: POET, LLC
competitors.note: Largest US ethanol producer, competing with Valero's 12 ethanol plants.

threats: Normalisation of the record 2026 crack spreads once Middle East supply and Strait of Hormuz flows recover, which could cut earnings sharply (consensus already sees revenue and EPS falling in 2027 and 2028).
Long-term decline in gasoline demand from electric vehicles and better fuel economy in the US and Europe.
New large export refineries in the Middle East, India, Africa (Dangote) and Mexico (Dos Bocas) competing for Valero's Latin American export markets.
California and other state regulations that raise costs and force closures (Benicia idled April 2026; Benicia and Wilmington impairments of $1,131M in 2025).
Changes to the Renewable Fuel Standard, small-refinery exemptions and biofuel tax credits (45Z) that affect RIN costs and renewable diesel and SAF margins.
Process-safety incidents or hurricanes hitting its concentrated Gulf Coast refinery base.

ceo.name: R. Lane Riggs
ceo.background: Chemical engineer (BS, University of Oklahoma) with an MBA from West Texas A&M; joined in 1989 as a process engineer at the McKee refinery, rose through refining operations to President and COO, CEO since June 30, 2023 and Chairman since December 31, 2024

c1.evidence: Petroleum refining is a mature, century-old industry, and Valero's revenue fell from $176,383M in 2022 to $122,687M in 2025.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Valero mainly for reliable supply and price from low-cost, high-complexity Gulf Coast refineries; that scale is hard to replicate but gives no product differentiation.

c3.evidence: Many Americans know the Valero gas-station sign and Valero is one of the two largest US refiners, but it is not a beloved consumer brand people recommend.

c4.evidence: Valero publishes no formal mission statement; its stated vision is providing reliable and affordable energy with 'unmatched execution', which is an operating goal rather than an inspiring purpose.

c6.evidence: “gas station, oil refiner, polluter” — the public mostly sees Valero as a fuel and gas-station brand, with mixed-to-negative environmental views typical of oil companies.

c7.evidence: The global fuels market is huge but not secularly growing in Valero's core US and European markets, where EVs and efficiency weigh on gasoline demand; renewable diesel and SAF are growing but small (FY2025 renewable diesel segment revenue $2,508M).

c8.evidence: Valero has added renewable diesel (Diamond Green Diesel, up to 1.2 billion gallons/year) and neat SAF ($297M of 2025 sales), but these are modest next to refining, which was 95% of FY2025 revenue.

m1.evidence: Lane Riggs is an operations-focused CEO whose stated priorities are safe, reliable operations, capital discipline and shareholder returns, not a new vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Riggs is not a founder but a 37-year company veteran who rose from process engineer, showing long-term commitment to the business.

m4.evidence: Valero emphasises a 'Caring' value and safety-first culture (record employee TRIR of 0.13 in 2025), but there is little public evidence of a servant-leadership style specific to the CEO.

m5.evidence: Valero's culture is built around operational excellence and safety rather than inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Riggs is a chemical engineer who started as a process engineer at the McKee refinery and led refining operations and engineering before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: There are no known controversies about Riggs, but there is little public evidence on his personal mission beyond running the company well.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Lane Riggs giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Riggs keeps a low public profile typical of refining executives.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in mid-2023, Valero posted record refinery mechanical availability (97.5% in 2025), completed the Port Arthur SAF project and cut diluted shares from 353M (2023) to 294M (Q2 2026).

m10.evidence: Valero is known for capital discipline and low costs (2025 capital investments of about $1.9 billion including turnarounds), but not for famous frugality symbols.

c10.evidence: Its fuels power cars, trucks, planes and farms for millions of people in North America, Latin America and Europe, but the product is a replaceable commodity.

p2.evidence: Running complex refineries safely is technically demanding and fuels are essential to the economy, but many companies can do it.

f2.evidence: Operating margin peaked at 8.9% in 2022 and fell to 2.6% in 2025; it does not show a steady rise.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 total debt and finance leases were $11,349M against $7,874M cash and $25,001M stockholders' equity, with a net debt-to-capitalization of 11%, so debt is manageable but exceeds cash.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from -$1,579M (2020) to $15,690M (2022) and back down to $3,181M (2025), and operating cash flow from $12,574M (2022) to $5,826M (2025).

v1.evidence: Valero's gasoline and diesel meet the same specifications as rivals' fuels, so ordinary buyers have no product reason to prefer it.

v2.evidence: Valero has a strong safety culture and has been an Extel (formerly Institutional Investor) Most Honored Company nine straight years, but it is absent from major current best-places-to-work rankings.

c5.evidence: If Valero vanished, fuel prices would spike in the US Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent and its export markets until others filled the gap, but its role could eventually be replaced and fossil fuels carry environmental costs.
